summary: This StatPearls chapter, Epidemiology of Prevention of Communicable Diseases by Peter F. Edemekong and Ben Huang (last updated October 24, 2022), defines communicable diseases and their common modes of spread. It focuses on hepatitis A (HAV), covering its transmission, clinical features, diagnosis, treatment, and US and Florida incidence, and it closes with recommendations for vaccination and the role of the healthcare team in preventing spread.
one_line: StatPearls chapter on communicable disease epidemiology and prevention, centered on hepatitis A transmission, incidence, clinical features, and vaccination.
key_facts: Communicable diseases are illnesses caused by viruses or bacteria that people spread to one another through contact with contaminated surfaces, bodily fluids, blood products, insect bites, or through the air.
Examples of communicable diseases named in the note include HIV, hepatitis A, B and C, measles, salmonella, and blood-borne illnesses.
Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is preventable through vaccination and affects the liver causing jaundice.
The HAV test of choice for diagnosis is IgM anti-hepatitis A virus.
Stool concentrations of HAV are highest 2 weeks after transmission, and patients are considered non-infectious about a week after inoculation or the onset of jaundice.
In 2015, 1390 cases of hepatitis A were reported from 50 states to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a 12.2% increase from 2014.
The overall incidence of hepatitis A in the United States in 2015 was 0.4 cases per 100,000 population, the same as in 2014.
Overall, there has been a 95% decline in HAV in the United States since the HAV vaccine became available in 1995.
Florida reported 217 hepatitis A cases since January 2017, compared with a past 5-year average of 94 cases.
About 60% of hepatitis A cases in Florida required hospitalization.
The median age of reported Florida hepatitis A cases was 38 years, with the highest rates among people ages 25 to 44 years.
In Florida, Southeast Florida (Broward and Miami-Dade counties) had the most HAV cases, with 69% among males.
For presumptive treatment, an unvaccinated person with recent HAV exposure within 2 weeks may receive HAV vaccine or immune globulin.
Confirmed acute HAV infection is managed with supportive and conservative management, while worsening jaundice and encephalopathy call for liver transplant.

Recommended two-dose HAV vaccination, 6 to 12 months apart, applies to men who have sex with men, people who use drugs, persons with chronic liver disease, and persons traveling to or working in countries with high or intermediate hepatitis A endemicity.
